items.title: Here Are All the Surprise Star Cameos in Taylor Swift’s 2026 CMA Awards Performance
items.summary:
Man, it’s been awhile – 13 years to be exact – since Taylor Swift last performed at the CMA Awards, but when she returned to take the stage at the Bridgestone Arena in Nashville on Wednesday (Nov. 18), she did it in style and made sure it sparkled not only thanks to her sequined outfit, but with literal stars – country music stars, that is.

Related 

2026 CMA Performances, Ranked 

The whimsical performance – a mashup of her Toy Story 5 hit (which has topped the Billboard Hot 100 for two weeks so far) “I Knew It, I Knew You” and “Our Song” (No. 16 peak) from her self-titled 2006 debut album – kicked off backstage in her dressing room. Eagle-eyed Swifties likely noticed that quite a few of her debut-era outfits were strategically placed around the space. But look a little closer, and viewers might see that she had a very small but special – albeit not breathing – guest in the room: Jessie the doll from the Toy Story franchise.

That was just the first of numerous surprise sightings throughout the performance, which included several nods to the film series, including the backup dancers who were an homage to Woody, the blue sky and fluffy white clouds on the front of her guitar that harken back to the wallpaper in Andy’s room, the tree on stage that brought viewers back to Tire Swing Hill, and of course, the 14-time Grammy winner’s glittery, Jessie-inspired cowgirl outfit.

items.title: Travis Kelce Couldn’t Join Taylor Swift at the 2026 CMA Awards, But Here’s Proof He Was There in Spirit
items.summary:
As we swing into holiday party season, it’s important to remember that your significant other can’t always make it to every event. Take Travis Kelce . The Kansas City Chiefs tight end who is nursing a high-ankle sprain and a recent calf injury as he preps for Sunday’s (Nov. 22) showdown with the lowly Arizona Cardinals was not able to get a hall pass to zip down to Nashville for Wednesday night’s (Nov. 18) 2026 CMA Awards.

But just because he couldn’t be on hand in person to cheer on wife Taylor Swift as she took the stage for her first CMA performance in 13 years for a run through her Toy Story 5 hit “I Knew It, I Knew You,” doesn’t mean he wasn’t there in spirit and in the likes. Kelce showed up in the likes for a post from the Taylornation account featuring the star-studded intro to Swift’s set.

Not to worry, even though the newlyweds were apart, Swift had plenty of company as she made her way through the tunnels at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, bumping into Brad Paisley, Little Big Town, Eric Church, Lainey Wilson, Brooks & Dunn and Bill Anderson as she sang the wistful tune. She finally made her way to the stage in her Jessie the cowgirl-inspired outfit, where she was joined by a banjo-strumming Keith Urban for the performance that also mixed in a bit of her No. 16 Billboard Hot 100 tune “Our Song” from her 2006 debut album.

While the power couple couldn’t be together on Wednesday, Swift walked the carpet with Brittany Mahomes, wife of Trav’s teammate, KC QB Patrick Mahomes. The couple were also on host Paisley’s mind when he joked about Swift and Kelce’s…
items.t: Travis Kelce Couldn’t Join Taylor Swift at the 2026 CMA Awards, But Here’s Proof He Was There in Spirit

items.title: Beabadoobee announces surprise new album ‘Bananas 4 Cats’ with sweet single ‘No Punctuation’
items.summary:
Beabadoobee has announced a surprise new album, ‘Bananas 4 Cats’ – listen to the single ‘No Punctuation’ below.

READ MORE: Beabadoobee live in London: Four albums in, she’s reached arena headline status her own way 

The singer-songwriter is due to release her fifth studio record on February 19 via Dirty Hit/Interscope. It’ll come just five months after she dropped her previous LP, ‘Pylon’ , in September.

She teased the title of the forthcoming album during her headline show at London’s O2 last night (Wednesday November 18). Bea Laus also previewed ‘No Punctuation’ in the encore, telling fans that it would be out today (Thursday November 19).

The track is a gentle, acoustic guitar-driven number on which she sweetly sings about her partner: “ ‘Cause you are everything .” ‘No Punctuation’ dates back more than four years, with early versions previously appearing online.

View this post on Instagram 

Laus has been road-testing the single at recent UK gigs on her current ‘Powerlines’ tour .

Explaining how ‘Bananas 4 Cats’ came together, she explained: “I just needed to write an album like this after ‘Pylon’. It happened naturally; I got back home and felt inspired, and made another album.”

According to a press release, the “overriding theme” of Laus’ next LP is “home”. It adds: “Whereas its predecessor was written, recorded and about being on the road, with an extensive cast of collaborators, the new album was written and recorded in east London, in Bea’s living room, with just her friend, her partner and her cats.”

items.title: Ella Langley Reacts to Her Record-Breaking CMA Awards Wins: ‘Hard to Put This Night Into Words’
items.summary:
Ella Langley dominated the CMA Awards on Wednesday (Nov. 18), earning her first entertainer of the year win, but also picking up victories in categories including female vocalist of the year, album of the year ( Dandelion ) and single, song and music video of the year (“Choosin’ Texas”).

Related 

Ella Langley & More Record-Setters at the 2026 CMA Awards 

Here Are the 2026 CMA Awards Winners: Full List 

Best Photos From 2026 CMA Awards Red Carpet: Taylor Swift, Lainey Wilson, Megan Moroney & More 

In the process, her six wins broke the CMA record for the most wins in a single night. The previous record was five wins in a single night, which was first set by Johnny Cash in 1969 and then tied by Vince Gill (1993), Alan Jackson (2002) and Lainey Wilson (2023).

After the ceremony wrapped, Langley expressed thanks to fans for the whirlwind success of the night, but also the whole year, acknowledging the meteoric career ascent that has resulted from fans’ love for “Choosin’ Texas” and Dandelion .

“Hard to put this night into words and what it means. Wow,” she wrote on Instagram in the early morning hours of Thursday (Nov. 19). “Walking up on stage I have so many things going through my mind of what I want to say, but tonight was hard to come up with the right words. I want to say thank you to my fans. Thank you for loving this record, thank you for coming to my shows, thank you for believing in my artistry. This year has been the most incredible journey, and I want to thank you for sharing in that with me. I love y’all.”

items.title: ‘They Had Never Seen Anything Like Us’: The-B2s Take Manhattan in Preview of ‘New Wave’ Docuseries
items.summary:
If you’re not a football family – or if you need a respite from the NFL’s Turkey Day takeover – MGM+ has just the counterprogramming for you. Come Monday (Nov. 23), the streaming service debuts New Wave, a four-part music series about (you guessed it) new wave music. Beginning in the late ’70s, the alternative music genre – which sprung up everywhere from New York City to Akron, Ohio — melded punk energy, pop hooks and then-novel digital technologies to create a sonic and visual landscape that was as weird as it was wonderful.

Ahead of its premiere, Billboard is sharing an exclusive clip from the first episode, which features Fred Schneider and Kate Pierson of The-B2s.

“We were not living in New York City. We still were in Athens (Georgia) in our little bubble. We were just a larger group of friends hanging out being bohemian,” Pierson says in this new interview filmed for the series. “It just happened spontaneously, started picking up instruments.”

“It became a hobby, but then our friends started saying, ‘Play our house, play our party,’” Schneider recalls in the clip, which features plenty of vintage footage of the kitsch-loving rock band. “Someone said we should go play Max’s Kansas City, the club in New York City. We saved all our money, packed a station wagon — somehow we got everything in it, I don’t know how, don’t ask me — so we drove up. They had never seen anything like us.”

Like many of the other musicians interviewed for New Wave – Billy Idol, Mark Mothersbaugh of Devo, Stewart Copeland of The Police, Chris Frantz of Talking Heads, Kathy Valentine of the…
items.t: ‘They Had Never Seen Anything Like Us’: The-B2s Take Manhattan in Preview of ‘New Wave’ Docuseries

The nominations for the 69th Annual Grammy Awards were announced earlier this week, and not only were many of the biggest names of 2026 involved in the biggest categories, they were nominated all the way across those categories: Taylor Swift, Ella Langley, Rosalía, RAYE, Bruno Mars and Olivias Dean and Rodrigo were all nominated for each of album, song and record of the year. While those long-established titans and rising world-beaters found their names called early and often on Monday, other A-listers like Noah Kahan and Harry Styles weren’t as fortunate, while stars like Charli xcx and Madonna did get their share of nominations, but were arguably still left wanting for more. 

On this episode of the Greatest Pop Stars podcast, host Andrew Unterberger is joined by Billboard senior charts/data analyst Eric Frankenberg to break down how things shook out among the contemporary pop greats during this year’s Grammy nominations. We talk about the big-picture takeaways from the artists who were and weren’t recognized in the biggest categories, and what early leans we have about who will actually emerge triumphant on Music’s Biggest Night. 

Along the way, we answer all the biggest questions about pop stars at this year’s Grammys: Is Olivia Rodrigo the most likely frontrunner in album of the year? Could RAYE or Rosalía end up playing spoiler there? Did Confessions II deserve a crack at the top prize? Is Taylor Swift’s energy mostly going behind a different category this year? items.title: Grimes calls out Elon Musk over AI “sex slave” and urges him to “step up”, “do better” and be “the king he used to be”
items.summary:
Grimes has called out Elon Musk over his endorsement of a new AI ‘influencer’, while telling him to “step up” and “do better”.

The Canadian artist – who shares three children with ex-partner Musk – engaged in a back-and-forth with the tech billionaire and Tesla CEO via social media yesterday (Wednesday November 18).

READ MORE:  I used Grimes’ AI vocals to make a hit – here’s how I did it  

Musk took to X – which he has owned since 2022 – to post a video about an ‘influencer’ who’s fully generated by artificial intelligence, ‘Claudia’. “Super intelligence will hack your limbic system,” he wrote.

In the replies, Grimes (real name Claire Boucher) responded: “The fixation on fake women feels like cope. I’m a fan of Claudia, but she doesn’t have a birkin deal, and she isn’t a she; she’s an alien creature who’s both blessed and haunted by the entirety of ancestral memory.

items.title: Belfast Duo CHALK Is Killing It on Fontaines D.C.’s European Tour: ‘Performing Live Is the Core of Our Band’
items.summary:
You can read CHALK’s “Get Fucked,” their monstrous 2026 single, in two ways. The first is as a hedonistic anthem about chasing a dopamine rush amidst the crushing existence of late-stage capitalism: “Get a job, go to work, feels right,” lead singer Ross Cullen barks, adding, “Get yourself a new apartment, seems nice.”

The second is as a confrontational challenge — with the song’s incendiary title being repeated like a mantra in the song’s final stretch. Cullen has sown the seeds of this distrust of the song’s subject: “You walk in the door, I see a lie.” His salvation – a new life and a “new God” – might not quite live up to expectations after all.

When the duo performed it at Amsterdam’s 17,000-capacity Ziggo Dome in mid-November, it felt like all of the above and more. As the squelching synth line pinged around the venue, the pummeling monochromatic light show came with the brash confidence of a band that feels like they belong in this room; hours after we speak, the group is deservedly crowned the best live act at the Northern Ireland Music Awards.

Since mid-October, the Belfast-formed duo has been the lead support on the European arena tour for Dublin’s Fontaines D.C. on their victory lap dates following the release of its chart-bothering LP Dopamine Chamber . A smattering of Chalk T-shirts can be spotted throughout the standing audience, proof that they’ve already left their mark at number key European cities. The booking makes for a potent one-two punch: Dopamine Chamber subtly leans into that synth-heavy world and packs a similarly dystopian feel. 

Chalk’s 2026…
items.t: Belfast Duo CHALK Is Killing It on Fontaines D.C.’s European Tour: ‘Performing Live Is the Core of Our Band’

items.title: Trance, prog synths, guttural screaming: Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages is the year’s wildest electronic album
items.summary:
(Warp)
The Milan producer revisits his youth as a straight-edge punk fan voyeuristically dabbling in rave – and finds a thrilling interzone between both genres

The opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni’s Bandcamp page is striking. “Lorenzo Senni was never a raver,” it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor’s ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm’s length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a “neon-hued chemical world”.

A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini’s hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled “rave voyeur” who “just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings”. Accordingly, his albums to date have dealt in what approving critics like to call deconstructions or interrogations of dance music rather than dance music itself: 2012’s Quantum Jelly and 2014’s Superimpositions featured what Senni called “pointillistic trance”, spinning the icy, staccato notes and arpeggiated synth lines of the genre’s epic breakdowns into lengthy, beatless tracks that never reached the climax implied. In her recent career, she’s played alongside the biggest pop spectacular on the planet as part of Taylor Swift ’s Eras Tour but also enlisted some of modern rock’s most celebrated names ( Hayley Williams , Turnstile ’s Brendan Yates, Deftones ’ Chino Moreno) on her latest LP ‘Pylon’ . Finally reaching the hallowed ground of an arena headliner in support of that fourth record, it’s a good time for Bea Laus to be tying all these sides together.

READ MORE:  Beabadoobee – ‘Pylon’ review: making peace with the mess of being in your mid-twenties 

“I remember playing here when I was 18 supporting The 1975 , and I couldn’t even imagine this would be on my cards,” she gushes in the encore before the whole crowd joins her in a singalong of whimsical acoustic number ‘The Way Things Go’. Where some of her peers have ascended to such levels within one album cycle, Beabadoobee’s journey has been slower. Tonight, playing with her band on a stage designed to look like an American freeway replete with dusty roadside foliage, a phone box pasted with ‘Missing’ signs bearing her likeness and a towering telephone pylon whose wires stretch and flicker out over the crowd, Laus has crafted an arena show that embraces her multiplicities. It’s not a pop gig or a rock gig, but a hybrid that satisfies both camps.

items.title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou
items.summary:
He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original

‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.”

Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles released, aims to establish the Cajun magus as one of the greats.

items.t: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou

items.title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
items.summary:
The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’

‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.”

On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers.”

items.title: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business
items.summary:
She threw a (metaphorical) brick through Spotify’s window and exposed industry failings with her ‘Butts for Tour Buses’ campaign. Now the singer is embracing her Irish roots with her new album’s fighting spirit

Kate Nash was standing on a fire truck in a showgirl outfit complete with white tights and pink G-string, shouting through a loudhailer about the music industry’s failure to pay artists fairly, when she wondered if she’d gone too far. It was 2024 and the truck, which made pit stops outside the London offices of Spotify and Live Nation, had a large black-and-white picture of Nash’s bum on the back along with the words “Butts for Tour Buses” – a reference to her newly launched OnlyFans account, which she was using to fund her tour.

That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a megaphone, so that relationship is over. I don’t think we’ll be making their New Music Friday feature.’ And we didn’t.” [see footnote]

items.title: Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this
items.summary:
Ulster Hall, Belfast
With two sets of fathers and sons now in the group, as they play all of Moseley Shoals on its 30th anniversary, the indie stalwarts have aged into seismic and soulful performers

‘It’s only 30 years ago,” Simon Fowler says of Moseley Shoals. He would seem to mean it, but 30 years makes Ocean Colour Scene’s breakthrough album as old now as Revolver was when they were making it. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage.

They walk on to Green Onions, fresh from the Crown Bar, and open with You’ve Got It Bad, all supreme Motown stomp. Fowler sings with a hand in his pocket and looks taken aback by the welcome. The casualness is a conduit: his voice has aged into something close to peak Joe Cocker, grained at the edges, honey underneath. Lining Your Pockets is more resounding than ever.

items.title: Paris Paloma review – arena-scale alt-pop drama from a singer on her way to bigger things
items.summary:
Bristol Beacon
The UK artist combines feminist fury with accessible melodies and a dramatic flair that sees her alternately pogoing and seeking out the wind machines at the prow of the stage

People are dancing to a song they don’t know, with flower garlands in their hair and their arms around their friends. This reaction to Fairy Dance, an unreleased track written about the community that has sprung up around her music, says a lot about the moment Paris Paloma finds herself in, and tonight’s show feels for all the world like a stepping stone to bigger things.

Throughout, Paloma leans in to the built-in drama of songs from her second album, The Fatal Flaw, which pairs ornate folk arrangements with the sort of arena-sized alt-pop production favoured by Florence + the Machine. With a sculpture inspired by surrealist Ithell Colquhoun’s Tree of Veins dominating the stage, she falls to her knees to deliver high notes and seeks out wind machines at the prow of the stage, her flowing crimson dress buffeted as if on a wintry moor.
